kp.k: Unverified AI drafting produced fabricated citations in three briefs
kp.d: The February 21, 2025 report records that defense counsel Rafael Ramirez admitted using generative AI to draft briefs containing nonexistent authorities on three separate occasions. At the January 3, 2025 hearing, he said he had previously used AI for tasks such as drafting agreements, did not know it could fabricate cases, and trusted apparently credible excerpts without verification. The May 28 order records that he did not dispute either the absence of verification or his Rule 11 violation. These are findings about specific filings, not measured model error rates.
qs: Mr. Ramirez admitted that he had relied on programs utilizing generative artificial intelligence ("AI") to draft the briefs.
As such, Mr. Ramirez did not conduct any further research, nor did he make any attempt to verify the existence of the generated citations.
Mr. Ramirez explained that he had used AI before to assist with legal matters, such as drafting agreements, and did not know that AI was capable of generating fictitious cases and citations.

kp.k: AI assistance does not remove lawyers' verification duties
kp.d: Magistrate Judge Dinsmore distinguishes permissible assistance with initial research from reliance on unverified generative output. Lawyers must check authorities' existence, validity, and current treatment regardless of whether they obtain them from AI or traditional sources. The report invokes established citation-checking practices and available tools, including KeyCite and Shepardization, rather than proposing a new AI-specific duty or prohibiting AI use.
qs: It is one thing to use AI to assist with initial research, and even non-legal AI programs may provide a helpful 30,000-foot view.
It is an entirely different thing, however, to rely on the output of a generative AI program without verifying the current treatment or validity—or, indeed, the very existence—of the case presented.
The Undersigned does not aim to suggest that AI is inherently bad or that its use by lawyers should be forbidden.

kp.k: Good faith does not excuse unreasonable legal inquiry
kp.d: The report applies Rule 11's objective reasonableness standard and finds that Ramirez failed to make the requisite inquiry into the law. His assertion that he acted without bad faith or malice, and his belief that generated excerpts looked valid, did not excuse the failure. The court treats verification as the submitting lawyer's responsibility rather than work to be shifted to opposing counsel or the court.
qs: It is abundantly clear that Mr. Ramirez did not make the requisite reasonable inquiry into the law.
That the AI-generated excerpts appeared valid to Mr. Ramirez does not relieve him of his duty to conduct a reasonable inquiry.
Good faith is not a defense to the imposition of Rule 11 sanctions.

kp.k: Final sanction was $6,000, not the recommended $15,000
kp.d: Dinsmore recommended a personal $15,000 sanction on February 21, 2025, calculated as $5,000 for each of three briefs. On May 28, 2025, Judge Hanlon adopted the report only in part and imposed $6,000 personally on Ramirez, payable to the Clerk by July 10, 2025. The report states that the court-initiated Rule 11 process did not permit awarding the plaintiff reimbursement of counsel's additional time, despite the plaintiff's request.
qs: $5,000 for each of the three briefs filed by Mr. Ramirez where he failed to appropriately verify the validity and accuracy of the case law he cited to the Court and opposing counsel.
The Court therefore ADOPTS in part Magistrate Judge Dinsmore's report and recommendation.
Mr. Ramirez is personally sanctioned $6,000 and shall pay that amount to the Clerk of the Court by July 10, 2025
However, the applicable Rule does not permit the Court to do so sua sponte.

kp.k: Deterrence justified penalties beyond earlier AI citation sanctions
kp.d: The report cites comparable sanctions of $2,000 in Gauthier, $2,500 in Mortazavi, and $5,000 in Mata. Dinsmore reasons that these lesser penalties had not deterred the conduct, using Ramirez's professed ignorance of hallucination risks to support the higher recommendation. Hanlon likewise cites the three separate filings and prior penalties up to $5,000 in concluding that $6,000 adequately deters repetition and comparable conduct. This is the judges' sanction rationale, not an empirical study of deterrence.
qs: Monetary sanctions ranging from $2,000 to $5,000 have been found appropriate in similar contexts to the present.

While this amount is at the higher end of the sanctions that have previously been imposed for similar conduct, Mr. Ramirez's professed ignorance of the propensity of the AI tools he was using to "hallucinate" citations is evidence that those lesser sanctions have been insufficient to deter the conduct.
The Court concludes that a sanction of $6,000 "suffices to deter repetition of the conduct or comparable conduct by others similarly situated."

kp.k: Training and reputational consequences mitigated but did not moot sanctions
kp.d: Ramirez argued that professional reputational harm made sanctions moot. Hanlon rejected that position but considered collateral consequences, the disciplinary referral, and steps toward responsible AI education when determining the penalty. The report records Ramirez's continuing legal education and continued use of products he had been assured would not fabricate citations; that assurance is reported as counsel's statement, not established product reliability.
qs: sanctions payable to the Court cannot become moot because of external consequences.
The Court also considers the collateral consequences that Mr. Ramirez has experienced, and may continue to experience, from having improperly relied on non-existent AI-generated legal citations.

Mr. Ramirez reported that he has since taken continuing legal education courses on the topic of AI use and continues to use AI products which he has been assured will not produce "hallucination cites."

kp.k: Fabricated authorities implicated competence, meritorious contentions, and candor
kp.d: Dinsmore identifies Indiana Rules of Professional Conduct 1.1, 3.1, and 3.3 as implicated, finding deficient competence and unfounded legal bases. For candor, he reasons that Ramirez acted knowingly because he knowingly failed to verify the law, and expresses the view that discipline is appropriate. He refers the matter to the Chief Judge for consideration of further discipline; the later order references referral to the Indiana attorney disciplinary commission. The document does not report a final disciplinary adjudication.
qs: It is clear that Mr. Ramirez failed to provide competent representation when he submitted false legal bases to the Court.
There is no merit in relying on non-existent cases, so Mr. Ramirez's conduct clearly disregards this Rule.
Moreover, Mr. Ramirez did so "knowingly"—he knowingly failed to fulfill his duty of verifying that the law he presented was "good law."

the Undersigned REFERS the matter of Mr. Ramirez's misconduct in this case to the Chief Judge pursuant to Local Rule of Disciplinary Enforcement 2(a) for consideration of any further discipline that may be appropriate.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Dinsmore presents AI as potentially useful for preliminary legal research, but not as a substitute for lawyers' verification of authorities; unverified reliance can produce sanctionable court filings.
pts.d: In the February 2025 report, Magistrate Judge Mark Dinsmore distinguishes AI-assisted initial research from reliance on generated authorities without checking their existence, validity and current treatment. He attributes three briefs containing nonexistent authorities to Ramirez's admitted use of generative AI without verification. His position is not that AI use should be prohibited, but that existing professional obligations continue to apply. He also concludes that Ramirez's conduct implicates Indiana's rules on competence, meritorious contentions and candor; those are the magistrate judge's disciplinary assessments, not a reported final disciplinary adjudication.

pts.k: Hanlon holds that repeated reliance on fabricated AI citations warrants personal financial sanctions and concludes that $6,000 is sufficient for deterrence in this case.
pts.d: Dinsmore recommended $15,000, or $5,000 for each of three briefs, reasoning that earlier sanctions had not sufficiently deterred comparable conduct. In the May 2025 order, Judge James Patrick Hanlon adopted the recommendation only in part and imposed $6,000 personally on Ramirez. Hanlon considered Ramirez's AI education, reputational consequences and disciplinary referral alongside deterrence. This is a case-specific judgment about sufficient deterrence, not an empirical finding that the sanction will prevent future misconduct. Hanlon rejected Ramirez's argument that reputational harm made sanctions moot.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on court filings, Ramirez's admissions, established verification duties and analogous sanctions cases, not model benchmarks or measured hallucination rates.
pts.d: Dinsmore reports finding unlocatable citations in three briefs and records Ramirez's January 3, 2025 admission that he used generative AI and did not verify its authorities. Ramirez attributed his reliance to apparently credible excerpts and ignorance that AI could fabricate cases. Hanlon records that the failure to verify and the Rule 11 violation were undisputed. Dinsmore cites Gauthier ($2,000), Mortazavi ($2,500) and Mata ($5,000) as sanctions comparators, together with preexisting legal authority requiring reasonable legal inquiry. His claim that AI can help with preliminary research is a judicial observation without a separate performance study. Ramirez's report that he now uses products assured not to hallucinate is his account of assurances, not a court finding about product reliability.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern present legal practice in 2024–2025 and condition acceptable AI use on reasonable human verification; no long-term market forecast is offered.
pts.d: The proceedings concern three briefs, including an October 29, 2024 filing, followed by the January 3, 2025 hearing, February 21 recommendation and May 28 final sanctions order. Dinsmore treats verification as a longstanding duty applicable regardless of whether a citation comes from AI or conventional research. Apparently valid excerpts and claimed good faith do not excuse failure to inquire. Hanlon's reduced sanction depends on the particular combination of repeated violations, remedial education and collateral consequences. The anticipated deterrent effect is prospective but has no specified measurement period.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Unverified AI-generated authorities expose counsel to financial, reputational and disciplinary consequences while burdening clients, opposing counsel and courts.
pts.d: Ramirez bears the $6,000 personal sanction and reported reputational harm. Dinsmore referred the misconduct to the Chief Judge; Hanlon subsequently noted an order referring it to the Indiana attorney disciplinary commission. Dinsmore characterized the representation of HoosierVac as incompetent and ordered Ramirez to notify its chief executive officer. Plaintiff sought reimbursement for additional attorney time responding to the briefs, but Dinsmore explained that fees could not be awarded through this sua sponte sanctions procedure. Both judges frame deterrence as protecting court processes and influencing similarly situated attorneys. The source offers no claim about aggregate legal employment, pricing or market structure.
